summary: This standards-track memo defines extra URIs for use with XML Digital Signatures, Encryption, and Canonicalization. The URIs name algorithms and kinds of keying information. It was replaced by RFC 6931.

eli5.summary: XML security tools need names to say which method is being used. This document adds more names to that list. It was later replaced by RFC 6931.

subtitle: Names for cryptographic algorithms and key types in XML signatures and encryption.

tldr.problem: XML signatures, encryption, and canonicalization standards need URIs to name algorithms and key information types. When upgrading XML Digital Signatures from Proposed Standard to Draft Standard, some algorithms had to be removed, but interest remained in alternatives and additional algorithms not in the core standard.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4051 provides a registry of URIs for additional hash algorithms, signature methods, encryption algorithms, canonicalization methods, and key information types. These URIs use a dedicated namespace to avoid changing the core standards.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can use additional cryptographic algorithms beyond the core standard by referencing their URIs. The document was later superseded by RFC 6931.

today: RFC 4051 was obsoleted by RFC 6931, which consolidates and updates the list of XML security algorithm identifiers. Most implementations now use RFC 6931 for the current set of URI definitions. However, the algorithms and URIs defined in RFC 4051 remain valid and in use; applications may encounter them in real-world XML documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4051 provides a reference list of Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) for algorithms and key types used with XML Digital Signatures, XML Encryption, and XML Canonicalization. These standards, published as W3C Recommendations and IETF standards, use URIs [RFC2396] to identify cryptographic algorithms and structural elements.

When XML Digital Signatures was advanced from Proposed Standard (RFC 3075) to Draft Standard (RFC 3275), some algorithms had to be removed to ensure proven interoperability. However, interest persisted in some of these algorithms and in additional algorithms suitable for XML security applications. RFC 4051 provides a convenient repository for such URIs and descriptions, using a separate namespace to avoid changing the main XMLDSIG and XMLENC specifications.
sections.eli5: XML security standards use special names (URIs) to say which encryption method is being used. This document lists more names for methods that people want to use but that are not in the main standard.

sections.title: Hash and Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 4051 defines URIs for several digest (hash) algorithms used in XML digital signatures. These include md5, sha224, and sha384, each identified by URIs in the http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more# namespace. A DigestMethod element in an XML signature specifies the hash algorithm using such a URI.

The document also provides URIs for HMAC (keyed-hash message authentication code) algorithms that combine a hash function with a secret key to create a message authentication code. These include hmac-md5, hmac-sha224, hmac-sha256, hmac-sha384, hmac-sha512, and hmac-ripemd160. HMAC algorithms take an optional HMACOutputLength parameter that specifies how many bits of the hash to include in the final output.

For security reasons, the specification notes that MD5 is NOT RECOMMENDED for use in RSA-MD5 signatures due to cryptographic advances, though MD5 in HMAC remains acceptable for now. Alternatives like SHA-256 or SHA-512 are preferred where applicable.
sections.eli5: Hash functions turn a message into a short fingerprint. HMAC adds a secret key so only people who know the secret can make the same fingerprint. The document names many different ones.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 4051 defines URIs for public-key signature algorithms that combine an asymmetric algorithm with a hash function. These include rsa-md5, rsa-sha256, rsa-sha384, rsa-sha512, and rsa-ripemd160, which use the RSA algorithm with different hash functions. A SignatureMethod element in an XML signature specifies which of these is used.

The document also includes URIs for ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) variants: ecdsa-sha1, ecdsa-sha224, ecdsa-sha256, ecdsa-sha384, and ecdsa-sha512. ECDSA is an elliptic curve analogue of the older DSA algorithm and offers similar security with smaller key sizes.

The document includes ESIGN signatures, a scheme based on integer factorization that is much faster than RSA and can be implemented on smart cards without special hardware. The specification notes that RSA-MD5 is NOT RECOMMENDED due to cryptographic advances, and SHA-based variants are preferred.
sections.eli5: Signatures prove you made something. Different algorithms use different math. RSA uses big numbers, ECDSA uses curves, ESIGN is fast. You pick which kind by name.

sections.title: Encryption and Canonicalization Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 4051 provides URIs for encryption algorithms used in XML Encryption. These include arcfour, a fast stream cipher compatible with RSA RC4; camellia128-cbc, camellia192-cbc, and camellia256-cbc, which are block ciphers with the same interface as AES but developed independently; and kw-camellia128, kw-camellia192, and kw-camellia256, which are key-wrap algorithms for securing encryption keys using Camellia. The document also includes psec-kem, a key encapsulation mechanism using elliptic curve encryption.

For canonicalization, the document preserves the URI for minimal canonicalization from the original XMLDSIG namespace, even though it was dropped from the Draft Standard due to lack of proven interoperability. The URI remains for reference, in case interest in this algorithm revives.

The XPointer transform algorithm allows XML signatures to reference a specific part of an XML document rather than the whole document, taking an XPointer expression as an explicit parameter.
sections.eli5: Encryption scrambles data so only people with the key can read it. These URIs name different scrambling methods and ways to protect encryption keys. Canonicalization is a way of standardizing XML so signatures do not break when formatting changes.

sections.title: KeyInfo Elements and Retrieval Methods
sections.content:
An XML digital signature includes a KeyInfo element that tells the verifier how to find or retrieve the public key needed to check the signature. RFC 4051 extends the KeyInfo mechanism in two ways.

First, it defines a new PKCS7signedData element type for use within KeyInfo. A PKCS #7 signedData structure can act as a bag of X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs). The binary PKCS #7 structure is base64-encoded and embedded in the XML. Any signer information in the structure is ignored, and only the certificates and CRLs are used.

Second, it provides URIs for additional KeyInfo element types that can be used as the Type attribute of RetrievalMethod, which tells an XML processor where to fetch key material. These include KeyValue, RetrievalMethod, KeyName, rawX509CRL, rawPGPKeyPacket, rawSPKISexp, PKCS7signedData, and rawPKCS7signedData. The Type attribute is mandatory for raw binary key formats (like rawX509CRL) because they are not self-describing XML.
sections.eli5: A signature has to say where to find the key used to make it. These URIs name different ways to carry or point to keys, including raw binary formats and structures that hold multiple certificates.

viz.caption: Digest algorithm families defined in RFC 4051

items.title: MD5
items.text: 128-bit hash; NOT RECOMMENDED for signatures due to cryptographic advances.

items.title: SHA-2 family
items.text: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512; stronger than MD5 and recommended.

items.title: HMAC variants
items.text: HMAC-MD5, HMAC-SHA*, HMAC-RIPEMD160; keyed hashes for authentication.

items.title: RIPEMD-160
items.text: 160-bit alternative to SHA-1; less common than SHA series.

items.label: RSA with hash
items.desc: Uses public-key cryptography with integer factorization; RSA-MD5 NOT RECOMMENDED.

items.label: Elliptic Curve DSA
items.desc: Smaller keys than RSA, similar security; uses elliptic curve math.

items.label: ESIGN signatures
items.desc: Fast alternative based on integer factorization; suitable for smart cards.
